note:
Doctor: Good morning. Come on in and have a seat. I see you're a 79-year-old male here after your second cycle of chemotherapy for colon cancer. How are you feeling?
Patient: Pretty tired, doctor. A little weak, but nothing terrible.
Doctor: Any fever or chills at home?
Patient: No fever. I took my temperature this morning and it was normal. No chills either.
Doctor: Any cough, burning when you pass urine, or mouth sores?
Patient: No cough, no burning, and my mouth feels fine.
Doctor: Good. Your blood work this morning shows your white count is low at 1.1, and the neutrophils, the cells that fight infection, are down to 0.6. That is neutropenia from the chemotherapy.
Patient: Is that dangerous?
Doctor: It raises your risk of infection, so we need to be careful. Let me examine you. Temperature is 98.4, blood pressure 128/76, pulse 78. Your mouth is clear, your lungs are clear, and the skin around your chest port looks clean with no redness.
Patient: That's a relief.
Doctor: My impression is chemotherapy-induced neutropenia without fever. We will hold your next cycle for one week and repeat the blood count in three days. With the following cycle I'll add pegfilgrastim 6 mg, one injection the day after chemotherapy, to protect your counts. Stay away from crowds and sick contacts, wash your hands often, and call us right away if your temperature reaches 100.4 or you get chills.
Patient: Okay, I'll call if anything changes.
Doctor: Perfect. We will see you back in one week.
summary: A 79-year-old male receiving chemotherapy for colon cancer presented after his second cycle feeling tired and a little weak. He denied fever, chills, cough, burning when passing urine, and mouth sores. Blood work showed a white count of 1.1 and neutrophils of 0.6, and examination was unremarkable with temperature 98.4, blood pressure 128/76, and pulse 78. The impression was chemotherapy-induced neutropenia without fever. The next cycle will be held for one week, the blood count repeated in three days, and pegfilgrastim 6 mg added with the following cycle.

soap.subjective: 79-year-old male seen after his second cycle of chemotherapy for colon cancer, feeling tired and a little weak. Denies fever, chills, cough, burning when passing urine, and mouth sores. Temperature taken at home this morning was normal.
soap.objective: Temperature 98.4, blood pressure 128/76, pulse 78. White count 1.1 and neutrophils 0.6. Mouth clear, lungs clear, and skin around the chest port clean with no redness.
plan: Hold the next chemotherapy cycle for one week
Repeat the blood count in three days
Add pegfilgrastim 6 mg, one injection the day after chemotherapy, with the following cycle
Avoid crowds and sick contacts and wash hands often
Call right away for a temperature of 100.4 or chills
Return to clinic in one week

medications.frequency: one injection the day after chemotherapy

note:
Doctor: Hi there, what brings you in today?
Patient: My right eye has been red and gooey for two days. This morning it was crusted shut when I woke up.
Doctor: I see you're a 71-year-old male. Any change in your vision?
Patient: No, my vision is the same as always.
Doctor: Any eye pain, or does light bother you?
Patient: No pain, and light doesn't bother me. It's just itchy and gritty.
Doctor: Do you wear contact lenses?
Patient: No, just glasses.
Doctor: Has anyone around you had pink eye?
Patient: My grandson had it last week.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No known drug allergies.
Doctor: Okay, let me take a look. Your vision is 20/25 in both eyes, which is normal for you. The right eye is diffusely red with thin yellow-white discharge along the lashes. The cornea is clear, the pupils are equal and reactive, and there is no swelling of the eyelids.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: This is acute bacterial conjunctivitis of the right eye. I'll prescribe erythromycin ointment, a thin ribbon in the right eye four times a day for five days. Use warm compresses, wash your hands often, and don't share towels. Come back or see an eye doctor if you have pain, light sensitivity, or any change in vision, or if it is not better in three days.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
summary: A 71-year-old male presented to urgent care with two days of a red, gooey right eye that was crusted shut this morning, with itching and a gritty feeling. He denied eye pain, light sensitivity, and any change in vision, and his grandson recently had pink eye. Examination showed a diffusely red right eye with thin yellow-white discharge, a clear cornea, reactive pupils, and normal vision. The diagnosis was acute bacterial conjunctivitis of the right eye. Erythromycin ointment was prescribed four times a day for five days along with hygiene advice and return precautions.

soap.subjective: 71-year-old male with two days of a red, gooey right eye that was crusted shut this morning, itchy and gritty. Denies eye pain, light bothering him, and any change in vision. Wears glasses, not contact lenses. Grandson had pink eye last week. No known drug allergies.
soap.objective: Vision 20/25 in both eyes. Right eye diffusely red with thin yellow-white discharge along the lashes. Cornea clear, pupils equal and reactive, no swelling of the eyelids.
soap.assessment: Acute bacterial conjunctivitis of the right eye.
plan: Erythromycin ointment, a thin ribbon in the right eye four times a day for five days
Warm compresses, frequent handwashing, and no sharing of towels
Return or see an eye doctor for pain, light sensitivity, or any change in vision
Return if not better in three days

medications.frequency: four times a day for five days

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. So you're a 75-year-old male, and I understand you hit your head falling off a ladder about six weeks ago. Tell me how you've been since then.
Patient: Well, doc, the headaches just won't go away. They're mostly across my forehead, and they come on most afternoons. I also get dizzy when I stand up too fast, and I can't concentrate on my crossword like I used to.
Doctor: Did you pass out when you fell?
Patient: No, I don't think so. I remember the whole thing. I was a little foggy for an hour or so, though.
Doctor: And the CT scan of your head in the emergency room?
Patient: They said it was normal, no bleeding.
Doctor: Right, I have that report here, and it showed no bleed and no fracture. Any vomiting, double vision, numbness, or weakness since then?
Patient: No vomiting, no double vision, and no numbness or weakness. Bright lights bother me a bit, and I'm sleeping badly, waking up at three in the morning.
Doctor: What medicines and supplements are you taking?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg every morning for blood pressure, and a baby aspirin, 81 mg daily. And I take ginkgo biloba 120 mg twice a day for my memory, plus fish oil, 1000 mg once daily.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure today is 136/80 with a pulse of 72, and it doesn't drop when you stand. On exam your cranial nerves are normal, strength and sensation are normal, your gait is steady, and the Romberg test is negative. Your MoCA today is 26 out of 30.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's mildly low on the concentration items, but that fits with a concussion at your age. My impression is post-concussion syndrome with headaches, dizziness, and sleep disturbance. The ginkgo biloba worries me because it can raise bleeding risk, especially with aspirin after a head injury, so I want you to stop it. Continue the fish oil, aspirin, and amlodipine as you are taking them. For sleep, start melatonin 3 mg at bedtime. I'm also ordering an MRI of the brain and referring you to vestibular therapy for the dizziness. Avoid ladders, driving when dizzy, and alcohol until you're better, and increase your activity gradually.
Patient: Okay, I'll stop the ginkgo tonight.
Doctor: Good. Let's see you back in six weeks, sooner if the headaches worsen, you vomit repeatedly, or you notice weakness or confusion.
summary: A 75-year-old male presented with persistent headaches, dizziness on standing, poor concentration, light sensitivity, and poor sleep since falling from a ladder about six weeks ago. He did not lose consciousness, and his emergency room head CT showed no bleed or fracture. He reported no vomiting, double vision, numbness, or weakness. Examination was normal with a MoCA of 26 out of 30, and the impression was post-concussion syndrome. Ginkgo biloba is stopped because of bleeding risk with aspirin, melatonin 3 mg is started at bedtime, an MRI of the brain is ordered, and vestibular therapy is arranged.

soap.subjective: 75-year-old male with persistent forehead headaches most afternoons, dizziness when standing quickly, difficulty concentrating, brief fogginess, light sensitivity, and poor sleep with early waking since falling off a ladder about six weeks ago. Did not pass out. Denies vomiting, double vision, numbness, and weakness. Takes amlodipine 5 mg every morning, aspirin 81 mg daily, ginkgo biloba 120 mg twice a day, and fish oil 1000 mg once daily.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 136/80, pulse 72, no drop on standing. Cranial nerves, strength, sensation, and gait normal, Romberg test negative. MoCA 26 out of 30. CT scan of the head after the fall showed no bleed and no fracture.
soap.assessment: Post-concussion syndrome with headaches, dizziness, and sleep disturbance.
plan: Stop ginkgo biloba because of bleeding risk with aspirin
Continue fish oil, aspirin, and amlodipine unchanged
Start melatonin 3 mg at bedtime
MRI of the brain
Refer to vestibular therapy for dizziness
Avoid ladders, driving when dizzy, and alcohol, and increase activity gradually
Return in six weeks, sooner for worsening headaches, repeated vomiting, weakness, or confusion

note: Endocrinology follow-up visit for an 18-year-old male referred for an incidentally discovered left adrenal mass. The mass was found on CT of the abdomen obtained in the emergency department after a bicycle crash three weeks ago, and it measures 2.1 cm with smooth margins, homogeneous appearance, and an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units. He has no history of hypertension and denies headaches, palpitations, episodic sweating, weight gain, easy bruising, and muscle weakness. He takes no regular medications and has no family history of endocrine tumors. On examination blood pressure is 118/72 and heart rate is 64. He has no cushingoid features, no abdominal striae, and no hirsutism. Plasma free metanephrines are normal and potassium is 4.2. The 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test gave a morning cortisol of 1.1 mcg/dL, which shows adequate suppression. An aldosterone to renin ratio was not ordered because he is normotensive with a normal potassium. Impression is a small, lipid-rich left adrenal incidentaloma that is hormonally nonfunctioning, with no evidence of pheochromocytoma or autonomous cortisol secretion. Given his age and the benign imaging features, we will avoid further radiation and repeat imaging with MRI of the adrenal glands in 12 months. We reviewed warning symptoms, including severe headaches, palpitations, or sweating, and he will call if they occur. Follow up in clinic in 12 months with the MRI results.
summary: An 18-year-old male was seen in endocrinology for an incidentally found left adrenal mass measuring 2.1 cm with an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units. He has no history of hypertension and denies headaches, palpitations, sweating, weight gain, easy bruising, and muscle weakness. Blood pressure was 118/72, plasma free metanephrines were normal, and the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test showed adequate suppression with a cortisol of 1.1 mcg/dL. The impression is a small, lipid-rich, hormonally nonfunctioning left adrenal incidentaloma. Repeat MRI of the adrenal glands is planned in 12 months with clinic follow-up.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I see you're a 66-year-old male with obstructive sleep apnea, here to review how the CPAP is going. Who did you bring with you today?
Patient: This is my wife. She sleeps down the hall from me these days.
Family member: Because he snores so loudly! On the nights he skips the machine I can hear him through the wall, and he stops breathing for a few seconds at a time.
Patient: I'll admit I only use it about three or four nights a week. The mask leaks and my mouth gets dry.
Doctor: Any morning headaches or falling asleep while driving?
Patient: No headaches, and I haven't nodded off at the wheel. I do get sleepy in the afternoon, though.
Doctor: Any chest pain or trouble breathing during the day?
Patient: None.
Doctor: Your machine download shows use on four of the last seven nights and a residual apnea-hypopnea index of 12 events per hour, with a high mask leak. Your blood pressure today is 134/80 and your oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. I see you take lisinopril 10 mg once daily.
Patient: That's right.
Doctor: My impression is obstructive sleep apnea with poor CPAP adherence because of mask leak and dry mouth. I'm going to have our respiratory therapist refit you for a full face mask, and I'll add a heated humidifier. Use saline nasal spray, two sprays in each nostril at bedtime. Please aim for every night, all night. We will recheck the machine download in four weeks and see you back in six weeks.
Family member: I'll make sure he wears it.
Patient: Okay, I'll try.
summary: A 66-year-old male with obstructive sleep apnea was seen to review CPAP use, accompanied by his wife who described loud snoring and pauses in breathing on nights he skips the machine. He uses it only three or four nights a week because of mask leak and dry mouth, and he feels sleepy in the afternoon but denies morning headaches, drowsy driving, and chest pain. The download showed use on four of seven nights and a residual apnea-hypopnea index of 12 with high mask leak. The impression is obstructive sleep apnea with poor CPAP adherence. A full face mask refit, a heated humidifier, and saline nasal spray were ordered, with a download recheck in four weeks.

note: Telehealth video visit, family medicine. The patient is a 63-year-old male who joined from home on a tablet with a good video and audio connection. He asked for help with sneezing and itchy, watery eyes that come back every spring. He said it started about three weeks ago when the trees began to bloom. He also has a runny nose, and the sneezing comes in long fits and is worse when he is outside or when the windows are open. He denies fever, facial pain, wheezing, and shortness of breath. He has not taken anything for it so far. He has hypertension and takes amlodipine 5 mg once daily. Because he has limited health literacy, I used plain language, avoided medical terms, and had him repeat the plan back to me, which he did correctly. He read his home blood pressure monitor to me as 128/78 with a pulse of 72. On video he looked comfortable, spoke in full sentences, and had no labored breathing. His eyes looked mildly red with clear tearing, and he rubbed his nose several times during the visit. There was no facial swelling. My impression is seasonal allergic rhinitis. I am starting fluticasone nasal spray, one spray in each nostril once daily, and I showed him on camera how to aim the tip toward the outer wall of the nose. I advised him to skip decongestant pills because of his blood pressure, keep the windows closed on high pollen days, and wash his face and change clothes after being outdoors. He should send a portal message or call if he develops wheezing, fever, or facial pain. We will follow up by video in three weeks.
summary: A 63-year-old male with hypertension was seen by video for sneezing, a runny nose, and itchy, watery eyes that began about three weeks ago and come back every spring. He denied fever, facial pain, wheezing, and shortness of breath, and he has not taken anything for it. On video he looked comfortable with mildly red eyes and clear tearing, and his home blood pressure was 128/78 with a pulse of 72. The impression was seasonal allergic rhinitis. Fluticasone nasal spray was started, with advice to avoid decongestant pills, limit pollen exposure, and follow up by video in three weeks.

note:
Hospital day 2 for this 89-year-old female admitted with symptomatic hyponatremia. Her daughter, who lives with her and manages her pills, is at the bedside and is providing part of the history.

Overnight she had no seizure, no falls, and no vomiting. She received a single 3% saline 100 mL bolus in the ED yesterday evening and has been on a 1.2 L fluid restriction since then. This morning she says her nausea is gone and she feels clearer, although she is still slow to answer questions. She denies headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, and ongoing diarrhea.

The daughter reports that they returned six days ago from a three-week trip overseas to visit relatives, ending with a long-haul flight home. During the trip the patient had about three days of loose stools that resolved on their own before the flight. The daughter says she drank a great deal of water and tea on the flight to stay hydrated, and over the next two days she became progressively confused, nauseated, and unsteady. There has been no alcohol use and no new supplements. The daughter first told me the patient takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. This morning she brought in the pill bottles and, correction, the label reads hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily, and that is the dose the patient has actually been taking. Her other home medications are sertraline 50 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and apixaban 2.5 mg BID. Past medical history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, atrial fibrillation, depression, and CKD stage 3.

Vitals this morning are BP 152/84, HR 76, RR 16, temp 36.8 C, and SpO2 96% on room air, with a weight of 54 kg. She is alert and oriented to person and place but not to time. Mucous membranes are moist, neck veins are flat, lungs are clear, and the heart rhythm is irregularly irregular with a controlled rate. There is no peripheral edema, and the neurologic exam is nonfocal with no asterixis. Sodium was 118 mEq/L on admission, 121 after the bolus, and 124 this morning, a rise of 6 mEq/L over about 15 hours. Serum osmolality is 254, urine osmolality 420, urine sodium elevated at forty-eight mEq/L, TSH 2.4, random cortisol 19, potassium 3.7, glucose 98, and creatinine 1.1 with an eGFR of 44. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute abnormality and CXR showed clear lungs without infiltrate.

Symptomatic hyponatremia, euvolemic on exam, is most likely thiazide-induced with contribution from sertraline and excess free water intake during the trip. TSH and cortisol are normal, which argues against an endocrine cause. I am discontinuing hydrochlorothiazide and she should avoid thiazide diuretics going forward. I am reducing sertraline from 50 mg to 25 mg daily. We will continue the 1.2 L fluid restriction, repeat a BMP every six hours today and then daily, and keep the goal rise to no more than eight mEq/L per 24 hours. If her confusion worsens or the level falls, I will repeat the 3% saline bolus.

For hypertension, BP is above goal, so I am starting amlodipine 2.5 mg daily in place of the hydrochlorothiazide. For atrial fibrillation, the rate is controlled without a rate-control agent and she will continue apixaban 2.5 mg BID, which is appropriate for her age over 80 and weight of 54 kg. For hypothyroidism, continue levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. For CKD stage 3, creatinine is 1.1, so I will avoid nephrotoxins and dose medications for her eGFR. Her confusion is improving, so delirium precautions continue and PT and OT will evaluate her today. If the level is stable we expect discharge in about two days with a BMP at the primary care office within one week. The daughter was updated at the bedside and understands the medication changes.
summary: An 89-year-old female on hospital day 2 for symptomatic hyponatremia, with her daughter providing part of the history, became confused, nauseated, and unsteady after a three-week overseas trip with loose stools and heavy water intake. Sodium was 118 mEq/L on admission and 124 this morning after a 3% saline bolus and fluid restriction, with normal TSH and cortisol and no acute imaging findings. The daughter's first report of hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg was corrected to 12.5 mg daily from the pill bottle. The impression is thiazide-induced hyponatremia with contribution from sertraline and free water intake. Hydrochlorothiazide is stopped, sertraline is reduced to 25 mg daily, amlodipine is started, and monitoring continues.

Sodium 118 mEq/L on admission, 121 after the 3% saline bolus, and 124 this morning. Serum osmolality 254, urine osmolality 420, urine sodium elevated at forty-eight mEq/L, TSH 2.4, random cortisol 19, potassium 3.7, glucose 98, creatinine 1.1, eGFR 44. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute abnormality; CXR showed clear lungs without infiltrate.
soap.assessment: Symptomatic hyponatremia, euvolemic on exam, most likely thiazide-induced with contribution from sertraline and excess free water intake during the trip. Hypertension above goal, atrial fibrillation with controlled rate, hypothyroidism with normal TSH, CKD stage 3, and improving confusion.

note:
Nephrology consultation requested by the hospitalist team for heavy proteinuria and leg swelling in a 60-year-old female.

HPI: The patient reports four weeks of progressive swelling of both legs, puffy eyelids in the morning, foamy urine, and a weight gain of about 5 kg. She denies gross hematuria, flank pain, fever, rash, and joint pain. She has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for ten years and takes metformin 500 mg BID. She takes no other medications and no over-the-counter pain relievers.

Exam: BP 142/86, HR 80, and she is afebrile. There is periorbital edema and 2+ pitting edema to the knees bilaterally. Lungs are clear, there is no JVD, and there is no rash.

Data: Urine protein to creatinine ratio is 7.2 g/g, and urinalysis shows 4+ protein, no blood, and oval fat bodies. Serum albumin is 1.9 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and total cholesterol 310 mg/dL. A1c is 7.1%. Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys with no hydronephrosis.

Impression: Nephrotic syndrome with preserved kidney function. The cause is not yet clear and needs a tissue diagnosis. Diabetic kidney disease is less likely given the rapid onset over weeks.

Recommendations: Ultrasound-guided renal biopsy once coagulation studies are back. Send ANA, complement C3 and C4, hepatitis B and C serologies, HIV, PLA2R antibody, and serum protein electrophoresis. Start furosemide 40 mg IV twice daily for the edema, with daily weights and a 2 g sodium diet. Continue metformin 500 mg BID while kidney function stays normal. We will follow along with you.
summary: A 60-year-old female with type 2 diabetes was seen in nephrology consultation for four weeks of leg swelling, puffy eyelids, foamy urine, and weight gain. She denied gross hematuria, flank pain, fever, rash, and joint pain. Urine protein to creatinine ratio was 7.2 g/g, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, with normal-sized kidneys on ultrasound. The impression is nephrotic syndrome with preserved kidney function and an unclear cause. A renal biopsy, serologic work-up, and furosemide 40 mg IV twice daily were recommended.

note:
This is an emergency department dictation on a 59-year-old male with an acute asthma attack. Chief complaint is shortness of breath and wheezing for one day. History is from the patient and from his wife who is at the bedside because he can only speak in short phrases. He has had asthma for many years and says he caught a cold with a runny nose and cough four days ago, then the wheezing and chest tightness started yesterday and got steadily worse overnight until he could not lie flat. He used his albuterol inhaler about every hour through the night with only brief relief. He denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain, and he has not been around anyone who is sick with the flu. Past medical history includes asthma, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, GERD, and obesity. His wife reads the medication list from her phone, fluticasone salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation twice daily, albuterol inhaler two puffs every four hours as needed, montelukast 10 mg nightly, lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, correction, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, she rechecked the bottle and it is 1000 twice daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. She also says he has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the past week for knee pain, and the patient confirms that. He has never smoked and rarely drinks alcohol.

On arrival blood pressure 158/92, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 89% on room air, temperature 37.1 Celsius, and peak flow 180 liters per minute. On exam he is sitting upright in a tripod position and speaks in two to three word phrases, with accessory muscle use, diffuse expiratory wheezes, a prolonged expiratory phase, and decreased air movement at both bases. No stridor, no cyanosis, no peripheral edema, and the heart is tachycardic but regular without a murmur.

ED course, he received three back to back albuterol ipratropium nebulizers, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV once, and magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes. After treatment his respiratory rate was 18, heart rate 92, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and peak flow 380 liters per minute. Labs show WBC 11.8, hemoglobin 14.6, platelets 245, glucose 248, potassium 3.4, and creatinine 1.0. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.36 and pCO2 42. Troponin was negative. Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation without infiltrate or pneumothorax, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes.

Medical decision making, this is a moderate to severe asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection and likely worsened by regular ibuprofen use. The hyperglycemia is from his diabetes and the stress of the illness, and the mild hypokalemia is from the albuterol. He was observed for four hours with no return of symptoms and was then safe for discharge. Plan is prednisone 40 mg daily for five days, and I am increasing his fluticasone salmeterol from 250/50 to 500/50, one inhalation twice daily. I am stopping the ibuprofen and he can use acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for knee pain. He will continue albuterol, montelukast, lisinopril, metformin, and omeprazole as before and check his blood sugar twice a day while on prednisone. He will see his primary care doctor in two to three days and pulmonology in two weeks, and return right away for worsening breathing, trouble speaking, or blue lips. His wife understands the plan and agrees.

After albuterol ipratropium nebulizers, methylprednisolone, and magnesium sulfate, his saturation was 96% and peak flow improved from 180 to 380. The impression was a moderate to severe asthma exacerbation worsened by ibuprofen. He was discharged on prednisone, a higher fluticasone salmeterol dose, and no ibuprofen, with early follow-up.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I'm the neurologist. I understand you're a 64-year-old female who had a seizure three weeks ago. Can you tell me what happened?
Patient: I honestly don't remember most of it. My husband says I was making breakfast, went quiet and stared at the wall, and then I fell down and my whole body stiffened and shook for a couple of minutes. I bit my tongue and wet myself.
Doctor: How long were you confused afterward?
Patient: About half an hour. I had a terrible headache and I was very sleepy for the rest of the day.
Doctor: Have you ever had a seizure before, or a head injury, stroke, or meningitis?
Patient: No, never. No head injury and no stroke that I know of.
Doctor: Any alcohol, drugs, fever, or missed meals before that morning?
Patient: No alcohol, no drugs, no fever, and I did eat breakfast. I smoke about half a pack a day, though.
Doctor: For how long?
Patient: Since I was twenty.
Doctor: Okay. The ER report says your CT of the head was normal, your glucose was 112, your sodium was 138, and the drug screen was negative. Now tell me what medicines you take.
Patient: Lisinopril 40 mg once a day. Actually, wait, let me look at the bottle. It says 10 mg. Sorry, 10 mg once a day. Then metformin 1000 mg twice a day, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and tiotropium 18 mcg every morning for my lungs. And tramadol 50 mg for my knees, about twice a day.
Doctor: Do you take all of those regularly?
Patient: Not really, doctor. The copay went up and I couldn't afford everything. I stopped the atorvastatin two months ago, I only use the tiotropium a few days a week, and I take the metformin once a day instead of twice.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me, we will work on the cost problem. Your A1c from the ER was 8.6 percent, which fits with that. Today your blood pressure is 164/96 and your pulse is 78. On exam your strength, sensation, reflexes, and walking are all normal, and I can see a healing laceration on the left side of your tongue. Your MRI of the brain last week showed only mild small vessel changes, with no tumor and no stroke, and your EEG today showed mild slowing over the left temporal region but no seizure activity.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It is not alarming, but it raises the chance of another seizure. My impression is a first unprovoked seizure, most likely starting in one area of the brain and then spreading to the whole brain. Your chance of having another one in the next two years is roughly forty to fifty percent without treatment, so I recommend starting levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day. It is a generic and inexpensive, and your creatinine of 0.9 means your kidneys can handle it.
Patient: Will it make me sleepy?
Doctor: Some people feel tired or irritable at first. Please stop the tramadol, because it can lower your seizure threshold, and use acetaminophen 500 mg up to three times a day as needed for your knees instead. Your blood pressure is too high, so increase your lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg once a day, keep taking amlodipine, and take the metformin twice a day again. For smoking I would like you to use a nicotine patch, 14 mg once a day. I am avoiding bupropion because it can also lower the seizure threshold. Your diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and COPD all need attention, so our social worker and pharmacist will review your prescriptions for cheaper options and copay assistance. I will also ask your primary care doctor to restart the atorvastatin as soon as it is affordable.
Patient: Okay. Can I drive?
Doctor: Not for now. No driving until you have been seizure free for six months, and no baths, swimming alone, or climbing ladders. If a seizure lasts more than five minutes, call 911. Let's see you back in six weeks.
Patient: Thank you, doctor. I will make sure to take the medicines.

She had no prior seizures, head injury, or alcohol or drug use, and she has skipped medications because of cost. Head CT was normal, MRI showed mild small vessel changes, and EEG showed mild left temporal slowing. The impression is a first unprovoked seizure. Levetiracetam and a nicotine patch were started, tramadol was stopped, lisinopril was increased to 20 mg daily, and social work will address medication costs.

note: Hospital day two progress dictation on a 78-year-old male with cellulitis of the right lower leg. He lives alone and has limited social support, no family nearby, and a neighbor who checks on him now and then. He was admitted two days ago with a red, warm, painful right shin and calf. Overnight he had no fever and no chills, and he says the pain is less and he is eating normally. He denies nausea, vomiting, and chest pain. He has no known drug allergies. Past history is chronic venous insufficiency with chronic leg swelling. His only medication is cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours. Vitals this morning temperature 37.2 Celsius, heart rate 82, blood pressure 132/74, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam the right lower leg has warm, mildly tender erythema, the marked border now measures 12 centimeters, correction, 11 centimeters, down from 15 centimeters on admission, and there is no abscess, no crepitus, and no skin necrosis. Foot pulses are palpable. Labs show white count 12.4, down from 14.6, and creatinine 0.9. Blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours. Impression is nonpurulent cellulitis of the right lower leg, improving on IV antibiotics. Plan is to continue cefazolin today, and if he stays afebrile tomorrow, transition to cephalexin 500 mg by mouth four times daily to finish a seven day course. Keep the leg elevated. Because he lives alone I am asking social work and physical therapy to evaluate him and arrange home health nursing for skin checks, and I want his discharge plan settled before he leaves. He will follow up with primary care in one week.

note:
Doctor: Hi, thanks for coming in. I see you're a 36-year-old female referred for trouble swallowing. When did this start?
Patient: About four months ago. At first it was only dry foods like bread and steak, but now even rice and pasta get stuck, and last week a pill stopped in my chest.
Doctor: Where does it get stuck?
Patient: Right behind my breastbone, about halfway down.
Doctor: Any trouble with liquids, or choking or coughing when you swallow?
Patient: Liquids are fine so far. No choking and no coughing when I drink.
Doctor: Any pain with swallowing, vomiting, or black stools?
Patient: No pain when I swallow, no vomiting, and no black stools. I've lost about eight pounds over the four months because I'm avoiding meat.
Doctor: And heartburn?
Patient: Yes, for years, mostly after dinner. I take omeprazole 20 mg every morning, but it isn't helping much lately.
Doctor: Any other medicines?
Patient: Apixaban 5 mg twice a day. I had a blood clot in my left leg two years ago and another one last year, so my hematologist wants me to stay on it.
Doctor: Good to know. Your blood pressure today is 116/72, pulse 74, and weight 61 kg. Your recent blood work showed hemoglobin 11.4, which is a little low. On exam your mouth and throat look normal, there are no neck masses, and your abdomen is soft and not tender.
Doctor: So my impression is progressive dysphagia to solids, most likely from a narrowing of the esophagus caused by acid reflux, although eosinophilic esophagitis is also possible. You need an upper endoscopy, an EGD, with biopsies and possibly stretching of the narrowing. Because of your history of DVT and the apixaban, I will coordinate with your hematologist. You will hold the apixaban for two days before the procedure and restart it the day after if there is no bleeding, and you will not need any bridging injections. Please do not stop it on your own.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense.
Doctor: I am also increasing your omeprazole from 20 mg to 40 mg every morning, taken thirty minutes before breakfast. Until the endoscopy, eat soft foods, cut food into small pieces, chew well, and do not lie down after taking pills. Go to the emergency room if you cannot swallow your saliva or liquids, or if you have chest pain or vomit blood. We will see you back about two weeks after the endoscopy.
Patient: Thank you.

She denied choking, coughing with swallowing, painful swallowing, vomiting, and black stools. Examination was normal and hemoglobin was a little low at 11.4. The impression is progressive dysphagia to solids, most likely from an esophageal narrowing due to acid reflux. An EGD with biopsies and possible dilation is planned with a two-day apixaban hold coordinated with hematology, and omeprazole is increased to 40 mg every morning.

note:
Neurology outpatient clinic dictation. This is a 76-year-old male seen for evaluation of a hand tremor that has been slowly getting worse over about eight years. He first noticed it when holding a cup or writing, and now he spills soup from a spoon and his handwriting is shaky. The tremor is in both hands, right worse than left, and it is not there when his hands are resting in his lap. A small glass of wine with dinner makes it better. He denies difficulty walking, falls, slowness of movement, and memory loss. His father had a similar tremor. He drinks four cups of coffee a day, correction, three cups a day. Past medical history includes hypertension and BPH. He has a documented allergy to metoprolol, which caused hives and wheezing, so we are avoiding beta blockers, including propranolol, even though it would otherwise be the first choice. Current medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily and tamsulosin 0.4 mg at bedtime. His primary care doctor started gabapentin 300 mg three times daily four months ago and he has had no benefit from it.

Vitals today are blood pressure 138/82 and heart rate 68. On exam mental status is normal, cranial nerves and eye movements are normal, and there is no masked facies. There is a moderate postural and kinetic tremor of both hands, right greater than left, with no rest tremor, no rigidity, and no bradykinesia. Finger-to-nose testing shows tremor but no dysmetria, and his spiral drawing is tremulous. Gait is normal with normal arm swing, tandem walking is steady, and Romberg is negative. TSH 2.1 and a basic metabolic panel from last month were normal.

Impression is essential tremor. This is not Parkinson disease because there is no rest tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia. Plan is to stop the gabapentin and start primidone 25 mg at bedtime, increasing to 50 mg at bedtime after one week if he tolerates it. I warned him about drowsiness, dizziness, and nausea with the first doses and asked him to take it only at night to start. He should cut his coffee to one or two cups a day, and I will refer him to occupational therapy for weighted utensils and handwriting aids. No imaging is needed. We will see him back in six weeks.

Gabapentin is stopped, primidone 25 mg at bedtime is started with titration after a week, caffeine is reduced, and occupational therapy and follow-up in six weeks are arranged.
